summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacles are whole-number bias (believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100') and the placeholder error (writing 25/1000 as 0.25). Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.

activities.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
steps: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
activities.insight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).

activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
steps: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.insight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.

activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
steps: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.insight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.

activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths
steps: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.insight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
steps: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.insight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.

checkQuestion: How many thousandths are in one hundredth, and how many thousandths are in one tenth? Then write 25 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal, and tell me why it is written that way.
checkAnswer: 10 thousandths in one hundredth; 100 thousandths in one tenth. 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025; the placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths (each place a tenth of the one before).
